problem: Existing embodied-AI simulators (AI2-THOR, Habitat, VirtualHome, CARLA, TDW, etc.) each cover a narrow slice of the world, such as home interiors or urban driving. They offer few scene types, few embodiments and weak multi-agent support, so agents are rarely trained or tested on unstructured open-world terrain, dynamic crowds or cross-embodiment transfer. The original UnrealCV is also too slow for real-time closed-loop and multi-agent interaction.
motivation: Generalizable spatial and social intelligence needs diverse 3D scenes, diverse bodies and multi-agent dynamics. Photo-realistic virtual worlds are also a cheap, safe way to expose failure modes before real deployment. Unreal Engine Marketplace scenes made by artists provide this diversity, but they need a fast Python/Gym interface to be usable for RL and VLM agents.
key_idea: The authors package 100 artist-made Unreal Engine scenes (indoor to 16 km² landscapes) and 60+ playable entities (humans, animals, robot dogs, cars, motorbikes, drone) as executable binaries. They drive them through an optimized UnrealCV+ plus a Gym toolkit, and use example navigation and tracking tasks to show that environment diversity improves generalization and that open-world challenges break current RL and VLM agents.
insight: At a fixed 100k-step offline dataset, spreading data over 8 environments instead of 1 (FlexibleRoom) or 2 generally improves active-tracking generalization to 16 unseen scenes, with the largest gains in Wilds and Palaces. It also transfers better to ThreeDWorld (SR 0.65→0.8). Per-environment gains are not uniform: e.g., StorageHouse 2 Envs 0.76 vs 8 Envs 0.64. The open-world settings expose weaknesses that curated indoor benchmarks hide. GPT-4o gets 0.00 SR on the multi-level Roof navigation scene, where humans get 1.00. Tracking SR falls from 0.92 at 30 FPS to 0.34 at 3 FPS, showing that perception-control latency matters. Moving a human-trained tracker to a robot-dog body drops SR from 0.68 to 0.48 with 4 distractors. VLM agents (GPT-4o, fine-tuned OpenVLA) are easily lured onto distractors in crowds.
method: Scene collection: 100 UE4/UE5 Marketplace scenes (35 landscape, 28 community, 23 building, 15 indoor; largest is 16 km²). Scenes are tagged by category, scale, spatial structure (multi-floor, steep, etc.), dynamics (weather, fire, fluids, doors) and cultural/era style. They are released as Win/Linux/macOS binaries because of licensing.

Playable entities: 19 humans, 27 animals, 3 cars, 14 quadruped robots, 3 motorcycles and 1 drone. Each has an egocentric camera (RGB/depth/normal/instance mask) and an animation-based locomotion system (Smart Locomotion: jump, climb, crouch, door opening). Each also has a NavMesh-based navigation system with sidewalk/road priority for autonomous NPC motion.

UnrealCV+: faster rendering and communication than UnrealCV. It parallelizes object-mask and depth rendering, adds a batch-command protocol for multi-agent calls and uses IPC sockets instead of TCP. Measured gains are object mask 70→154 FPS, depth 52→97 FPS, and 10-agent interaction 8→16 FPS.

Gym interface and toolkit: tasks are defined in JSON config files (agents, action spaces, cameras, reset areas). Wrappers provide environment augmentation, population control (distractor crowds) and time dilation (control-frequency simulation), plus a multi-env/multi-GPU launcher for distributed RL.

Example navigation baselines: an A3C online-RL agent (CNN mask encoder + FC256/LSTM128 + actor-critic) takes the egocentric segmentation mask plus the target's relative position. A GPT-4o agent is prompted with RGB plus relative position and outputs 3-action sequences. Both use a discrete move/turn/jump/crouch action space and are compared with human players.

Example tracking baselines: an offline RL (CQL) tracker following Zhong et al. 2024, trained on 100k-step datasets from 1, 2 or 8 environments collected by a perturbed state-based expert. Comparisons are PID, fine-tuned OpenVLA and GPT-4o, all acting with continuous linear/angular velocity.

setting.backbone: Navigation: A3C CNN+LSTM policy (trained from scratch) and GPT-4o (frozen, prompted). Tracking: CQL offline-RL CNN+LSTM policy (trained from scratch); OpenVLA (fine-tuned) and GPT-4o (frozen) as extra baselines.
setting.model_size: not stated (small CNN-LSTM policies); OpenVLA baseline is 7B; GPT-4o undisclosed
setting.training_data: Navigation: online A3C in each scene (Roof with 6 workers, Factory with 4 workers), trained and tested in the same scene. Tracking: three offline datasets of 100k steps each, collected by a state-based expert with multi-level perturbation. 1 Env = FlexibleRoom 100k; 2 Envs = FlexibleRoom + Supermarket, 50k each; 8 Envs = 12.5k from each of 8 scenes. OpenVLA was fine-tuned on the 8 Envs dataset. GPT-4o is training-free.
setting.observation: Nav RL: egocentric segmentation mask + target relative position; nav GPT-4o: egocentric RGB + target relative distance/direction/height. Tracking RL: egocentric segmentation mask; GPT-4o/OpenVLA: egocentric RGB.
setting.action_space: Navigation: discrete forward/backward 1 m/s, turn ±15°, jump (double jump = climb), crouch, hold. Tracking: continuous angular velocity [-30°, 30°]/s and linear velocity [-1, 1] m/s.
setting.simulator: UnrealZoo (Unreal Engine 4.27/5 + UnrealCV+); cross-platform test in ThreeDWorld
setting.privileged: Navigation agents receive the ground-truth relative position of the target (distance/direction, plus height for GPT-4o) and simulator-rendered segmentation masks. Navigation RL is trained and tested in the same scene with a fixed target. Tracking RL uses segmentation-mask input rendered by the simulator.

numbers_note: This is a simulator/platform paper, and the agents are simple baselines built by the authors. None of the numbers are on standard navigation benchmarks. The navigation table labels the second scene 'Industrial Area', while the text and appendix call it 'Factory'. Human reference navigation: Roof 515/1.00/0.97 and Industrial Area 158/1.00/0.98. PID, GPT-4o and OpenVLA tracking baselines are in the same distractor table: e.g., at 0D PID 113/298/0.34, GPT-4o 2/228/0.28, OpenVLA 55/323/0.10. Category-averaged SR over the 16 unseen tracking environments appears only in a figure. Per-environment 1/2/8 Envs results (16 environments) and 4D/8D/10D per-environment results are in appendix tables and were not transcribed. Real-world tracking (5 trials, all successful) reports AD/IoU of 764/328 for 1 Env and 833/393 for 8 Envs. AD is defined as pixel offset, where lower should be better, yet the paper claims 8 Envs is better, so these metrics look inconsistent. UnrealCV vs UnrealCV+ FPS: Color 74→83, Mask 70→154, Normal 109→131, Depth 52→97; multi-agent N=2/6/10 35→54, 13→25, 8→16.
results: UnrealCV+ roughly doubles throughput for object masks (70→154 FPS) and 10-agent interaction (8→16 FPS). In open-world navigation, the A3C agent reaches SR 0.32/SPL 0.10 on Roof and 0.52/0.31 on Industrial Area. GPT-4o gets 0.00 and 0.20 SR, and humans get 1.00 on both. In social tracking over 4 unseen scenes, the offline-RL tracker trained on 8 environments keeps SR 0.76/0.68/0.56 at 0/4/10 distractors, far above PID (0.34/0.30/0.14), GPT-4o (0.28/0.16/0.10) and fine-tuned OpenVLA (0.10/0.02/0.00). Its SR degrades when moved to a robot-dog body (0.48 at 4D) or run at low control rate (0.34 at 3 FPS vs 0.92 at 30 FPS).
limitations: Physics fidelity is limited: interactions are animation-based (binary door states, canned climb and jump), not physics-based. Interaction with objects and between agents is basic, with no manipulation or rich social behavior.
Marketplace licensing prevents releasing scene source code; only binaries are shared, which limits deep customization.

The experiments are small-scale demonstrations rather than standardized benchmarks. There are 2 navigation scenes with train/test in the same scene, a fixed target and a GT relative target position as input, 50 episodes each, and no instruction-following or ObjectNav-style protocol that could be compared with Habitat/MP3D results.
